servicesIndustries.name: Wholesale Trade
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Wholesale trade GDP contracted 1.2% month-over-month and 1.7% year-over-year in January 20261, with both readings negative and aligned with continued weakness in goods-producing flows. The decline tracks the -4.6% year-over-year contraction in manufacturing GDP2, as wholesalers of intermediate industrial goods face the same U.S. trade friction cited in the federal auto strategy.

Among the largest subsectors, farm product merchant wholesalers (NAICS 411), building material and supplies wholesaler-distributors (NAICS 416), and miscellaneous wholesaler-distributors (NAICS 418) represent the primary composition1. Wholesale trade is not tracked as a distinct project sector in the dashboard's capital project database, so the signal is GDP-only3. The jobs.json and procurement.json feeds are empty for the week of 2026-04-11, providing no direct hiring or contract-award signal for wholesale this cycle3. If cross-border tariff friction on manufactured and primary goods eases, wholesale turnover would recover in line with restored intermediate-goods flows.

servicesIndustries.name: Retail Trade
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Retail trade GDP rose 0.8% month-over-month and 2.7% year-over-year in January 20261, registering one of the stronger monthly gains among services industries as consumer spending flowed through to receipts. Statistics Canada's advance estimate points to February 2026 retail sales rising an additional 0.9% (based on a 53.4% response rate, subject to revision)2.

January 2026 retail sales were revised to C$69.7B, a +1.1% monthly increase, down from the initial +1.5% advance estimate2. Year-over-year February retail turnover was +1.5%2. Composition by subsector centres on motor vehicle and parts dealers (NAICS 441), food and beverage stores (NAICS 445), and general merchandise stores (NAICS 452)1. Retail is not tracked as a distinct project sector in projects_all.json, so the signal is GDP-only3. If interest rate levels and mortgage rate declines continue to feed through to discretionary spending, the monthly momentum in retail turnover would extend into the spring reading.

servicesIndustries.name: Transportation & Warehousing
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Transportation and warehousing GDP fell 0.7% month-over-month in January 2026 and remained +1.6% year-over-year1, as trade-flow volatility and port congestion pressured monthly throughput. Canada's freight and logistics market is sized at US$116.63B in 2026, with a projected CAGR of 4.45% to US$145.05B by 2031 (Mordor Intelligence)2.

Road freight held 60.97% of tonnage in 20252. Rail investments include 5,900 new grain hopper cars and extended sidings2. Vancouver port vessel wait times approached four days during January-February export surge periods, and multi-year on-dock rail and siding extension projects remain in carrier capex plans2. The project database tracks 236 transportation and warehousing projects valued at $41.8B3, concentrated in rail transportation (NAICS 482), truck transportation (NAICS 484), and warehousing and storage (NAICS 493). If port congestion eases and grain corridor flows normalize, the monthly drag on sector GDP would reverse in subsequent readings.

servicesIndustries.name: Information & Cultural Industries
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Information and cultural industries GDP expanded 0.9% month-over-month and 3.2% year-over-year in January 20261, tying with finance and insurance for the strongest services-sector annual reading and tracking accelerating AI infrastructure capital formation. The federal government launched a call for proposals on January 15, 2026 for sovereign large-scale AI data centres exceeding 100 MW through ISED2, with 44 affected projects flagged in the policy tracker.

Invest Ontario announced on April 8, 2026 that Microsoft is expanding AI infrastructure with two new data centres in York Region (Markham and Vaughan) supporting 1,250 jobs3. Construction began at 1452 McGill Road for Bell Canada's Bell AI Fabric national AI infrastructure platform on April 9, 20264. The CRTC released its February 2026 action plan on Canadian content and technology connectivity, with Online Streaming Act (Bill C-11) implementation continuing5. The project database tracks 44 information and telecom projects valued at $3.0B6, concentrated in telecommunications (NAICS 517) and data processing and hosting services (NAICS 518).

servicesIndustries.name: Finance & Insurance
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Finance and insurance GDP expanded 0.5% month-over-month and 3.2% year-over-year in January 20261, tying with information and cultural industries for the strongest services-sector annual reading. Q1 2026 bank earnings set records across the Big Six: RBC reported adjusted earnings of CAD$5.9B with EPS of $2.94 versus consensus of $2.812, and TD Canadian P&C net income reached $2,044M, up 12% year-over-year3. CIBC and National Bank also beat consensus, while BMO and Scotiabank met consensus2.

Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey for March 2026 reported that the combined finance, insurance, real estate, rental and leasing grouping lost 11,000 jobs — the first meaningful monthly decline since November 20234. Fitch's 2026 sector risk list cites geopolitics, trade tensions, and elevated consumer leverage5. Finance and insurance is not tracked as a distinct project sector in projects_all.json, so the signal is GDP-only6. Composition by subsector centres on credit intermediation (NAICS 522), insurance carriers (NAICS 524), and funds and other financial vehicles (NAICS 526).

servicesIndustries.name: Real Estate & Rental/Leasing
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Real estate and rental/leasing GDP declined 0.2% month-over-month and rose 1.2% year-over-year in January 20261, with the Bank of Canada policy rate holding at 2.25% and mortgage qualification conditions continuing to shape transaction volumes. CBRE projects $56B of Canadian commercial real estate investment in 2026 — the third-highest volume on record and +8% from the estimated $47B in 20252.

CBRE forecasts Toronto office vacancy falling to 13.4% from 15.9%, with 1.64M sq ft of new supply, and industrial net absorption above 20M sq ft in 2026; the CUSMA review scheduled for July 2026 is flagged as a key sensitivity2. Pension and REIT capital deployment reached roughly $15B in 2025 — about one-third of total investment, the largest share since 20212. BC Minister of Housing Christine Boyle issued March 2026 housing highlights and an April 2026 rental report, both linking to 114 affected BC residential projects in the policy tracker3. The project database tracks 285 real estate projects valued at $74.3B4.

servicesIndustries.name: Professional, Scientific & Technical Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Professional, scientific and technical services GDP edged down 0.1% month-over-month and 0.4% year-over-year in January 20261, as output softened despite continued hiring in the sector's sub-industries. Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey for March 2026 reported NAICS 54 employment gains of +12,000, one of the stronger services-industry gains for the month2.

Sector composition includes legal services (NAICS 5411), accounting and related services (NAICS 5412), architectural and engineering services (NAICS 5413), surveying and mapping, design services, management and technical consulting, scientific research and development, and advertising services3. Engineering and architectural services feed into data centre and construction capex cycles and into federal AI data centre feasibility work flagged in the ISED call for proposals4. Job Bank Ontario's sectoral profile indicates approximately 19% of the NAICS 54 workforce is over age 553. Professional services are not tracked as a distinct project sector in projects_all.json, so exposure is indirect — routed through upstream engineering, environmental assessment, and permitting work on infrastructure and energy projects5.

servicesIndustries.name: Management of Companies & Enterprises
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Management of companies and enterprises GDP fell 4.1% month-over-month and 21.9% year-over-year in January 20261 — the largest year-over-year contraction of any NAICS industry in the current StatCan GDP-by-industry release. The reading has been flagged for analyst review as an outlier relative to the rest of the industry set and remains unverified pending evaluation for potential head-office restructuring or reclassification effects2.

Sector composition is narrow: holding companies and head offices that manage subsidiaries, covered under NAICS 551, 5511, and 55111 (offices of holding companies)3. No project-level signal is available for NAICS 55 in the capital project database4. The jobs.json and procurement.json feeds provide no direct hiring-spike or contract-award corroboration for the management sector this cycle4. If the y/y figure reflects a reclassification shift rather than a structural decline in head-office activity, subsequent StatCan revisions would narrow the gap; the analyst note cautions against drawing conclusions from a single unverified reading.

servicesIndustries.name: Administrative & Waste Management Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Administrative and waste management services GDP was essentially flat in January 2026 at -0.1% month-over-month and -0.2% year-over-year1. Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey for March 2026 reported that the business, building and other support services grouping, which covers part of NAICS 56, lost 9,500 jobs, a 1.4% monthly decline2.

The sector is structurally dominated by micro-establishments: 52.1% of NAICS 56 establishments have fewer than five employees, 44.9% are small, and 2.6% are medium per ISED data3. The project database tracks 17 environment and remediation project records valued at $1.9B4, linked to waste management and remediation services (NAICS 562). Subsector composition also includes administrative and support services (NAICS 561) and services to buildings and dwellings (NAICS 5617)1. If business activity contracts further and regulatory assessment backlogs clear, waste and remediation capex would shift project pipeline composition toward environmental compliance work.

servicesIndustries.name: Educational Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Educational services GDP rose 0.5% month-over-month in January 2026 while the year-over-year reading remained at -1.9%1, reflecting the ongoing impact of federal international student cap policy on post-secondary enrolment. IRCC's 2026 international student cap is set at 309,670 study permit application spaces — 7% below the 2025 target of 437,000 and 16% below the 2024 target of 485,0002.

New international student admissions are projected to fall from 305,900 to 155,000, roughly a 50% reduction, while master's and doctoral students at public DLIs are exempt from PAL/TAL requirements as of January 1, 20262. British Columbia allocated $3.3B for post-secondary in its 2026 budget, a $600M year-over-year increase; McGill's redevelopment of the former Royal Victoria Hospital site is valued at $870M; and the University of Victoria's 510-bed residence broke ground in May 2026, with revised completion shifted from 2029 to 20343. The project database tracks 157 education projects valued at $14.7B4, concentrated in universities (NAICS 6113) and K-12 schools (NAICS 6111).

servicesIndustries.name: Health Care & Social Assistance
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Health care and social assistance GDP was flat month-over-month in January 2026 at 0.0% and rose 2.1% year-over-year1, as demographic demand and provincial capital commitments sustained sector expansion. Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey for March 2026 showed health care and social assistance added 5,000 jobs (+0.2%) on the month and 94,000 jobs year-over-year — the largest y/y employment gain of any industry2.

Ontario's long-term care commitment targets 58,000 new and upgraded beds over two years; as of March 31, 2025, 147 LTC projects / 23,977 beds had been completed, were under construction, or approved, and by February 2026 approximately 26,000 beds were open, under construction, or approved3. Quebec's 2026-27 budget allocates $2.3B for major hospital construction and expansion over 10 years, with 38% of Quebec's 594 hospital buildings classified 'poor' or 'very poor' as of early 20264. The project database tracks 259 healthcare projects valued at $20.5B5, spanning ambulatory care (NAICS 621), hospitals (NAICS 622), and nursing and residential care (NAICS 623).

servicesIndustries.name: Arts, Entertainment & Recreation
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Arts, entertainment and recreation GDP edged down 0.1% month-over-month and rose 2.2% year-over-year in January 20261, reflecting stable consumer discretionary spending and international tourism flows. Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey for March 2026 reported that the combined information, culture and recreation grouping, covering parts of NAICS 51 and 71, added 8,800 jobs, a 1.0% monthly gain2.

The sector's employment base is 402,100 workers nationwide as of 2024: amusement, gambling and recreation industries account for 68%, performing arts and spectator sports 25%, and heritage institutions 7%3. FIFA World Cup 2026 preparations include a $150M upgrade to BMO Field ahead of June 2026 matches4. The project database tracks 150 tourism and cultural projects valued at $22.3B5, including two ski resorts and two resort developments. Subsector composition spans performing arts and spectator sports (NAICS 711), heritage institutions (NAICS 712), and amusement, gambling and recreation industries (NAICS 713). If consumer spending on discretionary services holds and FIFA-related tourism flows through the summer, the year-over-year gain would extend.

servicesIndustries.name: Accommodation & Food Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Accommodation and food services GDP rose 0.7% month-over-month and 2.3% year-over-year in January 20261, as consumer spending on hospitality held up even as sector employment contracted. Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey for March 2026 reported accommodation and food services lost 10,000 jobs, a 0.9% monthly decline2, against an employment base of roughly 1.9M workers nationwide3.

Tourism revenue rose from $94B in 2022 to $109.5B in 2023 — a +16.5% two-year increase4. The 2024 vacancy rate for accommodation and food services stood at 3.8% (approximately 18,230 unfilled positions), versus a 3.1% all-industry average3. Sector composition covers accommodation services (NAICS 721), food services and drinking places (NAICS 722), and traveller accommodation (NAICS 7211)1. Accommodation and food services is not tracked as a distinct project sector in the dashboard database, so the signal is GDP-only; however, the FIFA World Cup 2026 hospitality demand flagged in NAICS 71 analysis would spill into 72 during the June-July match window5.

servicesIndustries.name: Other Services (except Public Administration)

Other services (except public administration) GDP rose 0.2% month-over-month and 0.3% year-over-year in January 20261, one of the smaller services-sector movements on an annual basis. Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey for March 2026 reported other services added 15,000 jobs on the month — the largest single-industry monthly gain in the March release2.

Sector composition covers repair and maintenance (NAICS 811, including motor vehicle and equipment repair), personal and laundry services (NAICS 812, including personal care, funeral, laundry and pet care), and religious, grantmaking, civic, professional and similar organizations (NAICS 813)1. NAICS 81 is not tracked as a distinct project sector in projects_all.json, so the signal is GDP and labour-force only3. The +15,000 hiring gain against the +0.2% monthly GDP reading indicates continued demand from household repair, personal services and community-sector activity; because these subsectors operate on thin capital intensity, the labour signal tends to lead the GDP print for NAICS 814.

servicesIndustries.name: Public Administration
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Public administration GDP declined 0.1% month-over-month and rose 0.7% year-over-year in January 20261, as federal workforce planning and defence-heavy capital allocation shaped the sector profile. The Carney government plan targets elimination of approximately 40,000 public service positions, with Employment and Social Development Canada projected to have 15,629 fewer staff in 2029 versus the prior year2.

The 'Canada Strong' 2025-2026 federal budget, delivered November 2025 by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, totals C$280B in spending over five years, with stated priorities on defence and capital investment3. Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey for March 2026 reported the natural resources sector added 10,000 jobs, an adjacent indicator of federal resource-policy capacity4. The project database tracks 233 public administration and defence projects valued at $165.1B, including 191 government and 15 defence records; defence is the largest aggregate-value government project bucket in the database5. Subsector composition spans federal (NAICS 911), provincial and territorial (NAICS 912), and local and municipal public administration (NAICS 913).
